citation: Andrew Russell and Lee Vinsel, 'Hail the maintainers' (dek: 'Capitalism excels at innovation but is failing at maintenance, and for most lives it is maintenance that matters more'), Aeon, 7 April 2016, edited by Sam Haselby, published in association with The Maintainers (an Aeon Partner). URL slug title: 'Innovation is overvalued. Maintenance often matters more'. https://aeon.co/essays/innovation-is-overvalued-maintenance-often-matters-more. Author bios at the time: Russell, dean and professor, College of Arts and Sciences, SUNY Polytechnic Institute, Utica NY; Vinsel, assistant professor of science and technology studies, Stevens Institute of Technology, Hoboken NJ.
evidence_tier: Essay (signed, edited magazine essay by two historians of technology; argumentative, no footnotes). Not peer-reviewed. Not an Egyptological source of any kind.
access_status: Fully read. Full text retrieved from aeon.co on 2026-11-28 (raw HTML downloaded and all body paragraphs extracted); about 2,900 words, no paywall.
exact_quotes: Opening paragraph: 'Innovation is a dominant ideology of our era, embraced in America by Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and the Washington DC political elite.'

Opening paragraph: 'What happens after innovation, they argue, is more important. Maintenance and repair, the building of infrastructures, the mundane labour that goes into sustaining functioning and efficient infrastructures, simply has more impact on people's daily lives than the vast majority of technological innovations.'
Paragraph on the 1960s: 'To take the place of progress, ‘innovation’, a smaller, and morally neutral, concept arose.'
Middle (history of the buzzword): 'At the turn of the millennium, in the world of business and technology, innovation had transformed into an erotic fetish.'
First of three answers: 'First, it is crucial to understand that technology is not innovation. Innovation is only a small piece of what happens with technology.'
Second answer: '‘Infrastructure’ is a most unglamorous term, the type of word that would have vanished from our lexicon long ago if it didn't point to something of immense social importance.'
Third answer: 'Third, focusing on infrastructure or on old, existing things rather than novel ones reminds us of the absolute centrality of the work that goes into keeping the entire world going.'

Same paragraph: 'Despite recurring fantasies about the end of work or the automation of everything, the central fact of our industrial civilisation is labour, and most of this work falls far outside the realm of innovation. Inventors and innovators are a small slice – perhaps somewhere around one per cent – of this workforce.'

Next paragraph: 'The most unappreciated and undervalued forms of technological labour are also the most ordinary: those who repair and maintain technologies that already exist, that were ‘innovated’ long ago. This shift in emphasis involves focusing on the constant processes of entropy and un-doing – which the media scholar Steven Jackson calls ‘broken world thinking’ – and the work we do to slow or halt them, rather than on the introduction of novel things.'
Same paragraph: '...fundamental vulnerabilities in our cyber-infrastructures are protected by the guards who work graveyard shifts and staff who repair fences and ID card-readers.'

Coinage paragraph: 'We can think of labour that goes into maintenance and repair as the work of the maintainers, those individuals whose work keeps ordinary existence going rather than introducing novel things. Brief reflection demonstrates that the vast majority of human labour, from laundry and trash removal to janitorial work and food preparation, is of this type: upkeep.'

Same paragraph, on Ruth Schwartz Cowan: 'new housekeeping technologies, which promised to save labour, literally created more work for mother as cleanliness standards rose, leaving women perpetually unable to keep up.'
Conference paragraph: 'More than 40 scholars answered a call for papers asking, ‘What is at stake if we move scholarship away from innovation and toward maintenance?’'

Late paragraph (self-caveat): 'One important topic of conversation is the danger of moving too triumphantly from innovation to maintenance. There is no point in keeping the practice of hero-worship that merely changes the cast of heroes without confronting some of the deeper problems underlying the innovation obsession.'
Closing: 'Ultimately, emphasising maintenance involves moving from buzzwords to values, and from means to ends.'
Closing: 'Innovation-speak worships at the altar of change, but it rarely asks who benefits, to what end?'
Final line: 'Our increasingly unequal and fearful world would be grateful.'
date_and_recency: Published 7 April 2016. Material discussed runs from Gordon's 1870-1940 growth period, the 1959 Kitchen Debate and the late-1950s Solow/Arrow work, through the 1970s-80s rise of 'innovation policy', to 2015-16 (Amtrak crash, December 2015 infrastructure bill, The Maintainers conference). Ten years old at time of research; the authors later expanded the argument in the book The Innovation Delusion (2020) [uncertain: book not opened for this item].
key_claims: Innovation is the dominant ideology of the era and is radically overvalued; what happens after innovation matters more.
Maintenance, repair and infrastructure upkeep have more impact on daily life than most technological innovations.
'Innovation' rose in the late 1960s as a smaller, morally neutral substitute for faith in 'progress', then became a buzzword, a fetish and finally a slogan exposed as hucksterism.

Three correctives: technology is not innovation (most technology in use is old, citing David Edgerton's Shock of the Old); recognise basic infrastructure; recognise that the central fact of industrial civilisation is labour, mostly outside innovation.
Inventors and innovators are perhaps around one per cent of the workforce; most labour is upkeep (laundry, trash removal, janitorial work, food preparation).

Maintenance means attending to 'the constant processes of entropy and un-doing' (Steven Jackson's 'broken world thinking') and 'the work we do to slow or halt them'. The framing is slowing decay, not ending it.
Maintenance work is disproportionately done by women and by low-wage and minority workers; the innovation focus obscures it (Ruth Schwartz Cowan, More Work for Mother, 1983).
Warning: swapping innovators for maintainers as the new heroes misses the point; hero-worship itself is part of the problem.
Innovation is value-agnostic (their example: crack cocaine in the 1980s); emphasising maintenance moves the conversation from means to ends and asks who benefits.
headline_figures: 'perhaps somewhere around one per cent' : share of the workforce who are inventors and innovators. Offered as an estimate, no source given.
'more than 90 times' : uses of the word 'innovation' in Richard Florida's The Rise of the Creative Class (2002).
'more than 250 books with “innovation” in the title… published in the last three months' : Wall Street Journal count, 2012.
'78 times' : appearances of 'infrastructure' on the programme of the American Anthropological Association annual meeting (2015).
'More than 40 scholars' : responses to The Maintainers conference call for papers.
'between 1870 and 1940' : Robert Gordon's period of unprecedented US growth.

Dates: Kitchen Debate 1959; Cowan's More Work for Mother 1983; Christensen's The Innovator's Dilemma 1997; Bierut essay 2005; Economist 2006; Nussbaum 31 Dec 2008; San Francisco Google bus protests 2013; infrastructure bill approved December 2015.
dating_and_context: Not applicable (a 2016 magazine essay, not archaeological material). Context: written to accompany The Maintainers, the conference and network Russell and Vinsel founded (the essay says they organised a conference; it does not give the venue or date in the text).
what_it_says_about_apophis: Nothing. The essay does not mention Apophis, Egypt, Ra, myth or ritual. Its only conceptual bridge is the phrase 'the constant processes of entropy and un-doing ... and the work we do to slow or halt them', which parallels a cosmos where chaos is repelled nightly and never finally destroyed. Any link to Apophis is the essayist's own analogy, not Russell and Vinsel's.
ritual_practice: Not applicable. No ritual is discussed. The nearest equivalents are mundane upkeep tasks the authors list (laundry, trash removal, janitorial work, food preparation, guards on graveyard shifts, staff who repair fences and ID card-readers).
prescribed_vs_attested_frequency: Not applicable. The essay gives no frequencies for any maintenance work; it describes upkeep as 'ceaseless' (of domestic labour, via Cowan) and entropy as 'constant'.
relevance_to_angle: Supports: the essay is the standard modern statement that keeping things going matters more than novelty, that decay is constant and work only slows it, that maintainers are mostly invisible, and that most of a workforce does upkeep, not invention. It fits 'chaos held off by routine work repeated' and the link to the heroic-developer essay. Complicates: (1) Russell and Vinsel explicitly warn against 'hero-worship that merely changes the cast of heroes', so the essay should not recast priests as heroic maintainers. (2) Where the analogy to Egyptian ritual breaks: their maintainers fix real physical decay (bridges, trains, fences) with measurable effects, whereas the Apophis ritual is symbolic action against a mythic threat whose efficacy cannot be shown; Egyptian ritual was elite temple work by literate priests, while Russell and Vinsel stress low-status, low-wage, often female or minority labour; the Egyptian ritual was performed to sustain an order (maat) regarded as given and good, while the essay's point is to ask 'who benefits, to what end?' of the systems being kept up; and their argument is a critique of capitalism's innovation ideology, which has no Egyptian counterpart. (3) The Egyptian case actually strengthens one point: the ritual of destroying Apophis is repeated precisely because the victory never sticks, matching 'slow or halt' rather than 'solve'. These breakpoints are the researcher's analysis, not claims in the source.
limitations_stated: The authors flag 'the danger of moving too triumphantly from innovation to maintenance' and that 'There is no point in keeping the practice of hero-worship that merely changes the cast of heroes'. They concede one argument 'Perhaps this point is cynical' (the crack cocaine example). They also criticise an over-correction toward object fetishism ('an equally superficial fascination with golf balls, refrigerators, and remote controls'). The one-per-cent figure is hedged ('perhaps somewhere around') and unsourced.
source_discrepancies: The page title is 'Hail the maintainers'; the URL slug and some citations use 'Innovation is overvalued. Maintenance often matters more'. Both refer to the same essay. The essay repeats the Wall Street Journal consultant quote twice (once as a pull quote). No conflicts with the Egyptological sources, since it makes no claims about Egypt.
verification_status: All quotes and figures above checked against the full essay text opened on aeon.co (2026-11-28). Figures the authors attribute to others (Florida's 90+ uses, WSJ's 250 books, AAA's 78 mentions, Gordon's 1870-1940) were not checked against those underlying sources [uncertain for the underlying facts, verified as what the essay says]. The 1% figure is the authors' own unsourced estimate. The reference to The Innovation Delusion (2020) in date_and_recency was not checked against the book [uncertain].
